issues.legal_issue: A pure question of law based on admitted or undisputed facts may be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court.
material_facts: The challenge based on the constitutional role of district planning bodies was raised for the first time before the Supreme Court.
The issue rested on facts admitted or established by the record and did not require an inquiry into new facts.
issues.conclusion: The Court entertained the new legal ground.
issues.legal_principle: A pure question of law that goes to the root of the matter may be raised at any stage when the facts are admitted or proved beyond controversy. The Court relied on Connecticut Fire Insurance Co. v. Kavanagh, Gurcharan Singh v. Kamla Singh, V.L.S. Finance Ltd. v. Union of India, Greater Mohali Area Development Authority v. Manju Jain, and National Textile Corporation Ltd. v. Naresh Kumar Badrikumar Jagad; it distinguished new factual pleas requiring investigation.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: A party has brought an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.pure_question_of_law: The proposed ground raises a legal issue that can be decided without investigating new facts.
predicates.facts_admitted_or_undisputed: The facts necessary to decide the proposed ground are admitted or established beyond controversy.

issues.definition: When an appeal presents a pure legal issue on admitted or undisputed facts, the legal ground may be entertained even if it was not raised earlier.

issues.legal_issue: A development authority cannot formulate a land-reconstituting town development scheme by taking over the planning role assigned to constitutionally recognized local bodies.
material_facts: The development authority formulated the scheme without obtaining the views or suggestions of the local bodies authorized to participate in planning.
The scheme involved changes to land use and the reconstitution of land.
A district planning committee had been constituted under state law.
issues.conclusion: The authority could not unilaterally formulate the scheme without taking account of the constitutionally authorized local bodies; doing so violated the governing statute and the constitutional scheme of local self-government.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 243G, 243W and 243ZD and Parts IX and IX-A of the Constitution provide for local self-government and district planning. Section 50(5) of the Madhya Pradesh (Chhattisgarh) Nagar Thatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973, as amended for the state, provides for a committee including local and planning representatives to consider objections and suggestions concerning a scheme involving plot reconstitution. The Court relied on Charan v. State of Maharashtra and the principles concerning district planning discussed in that decision.

predicates.town_development_scheme: A development authority has formulated a town development scheme.
predicates.scheme_reconstitutes_land: The scheme changes land use or reconstitutes plots.
predicates.local_planning_bodies_not_consulted: The authority formulated the scheme without obtaining or considering the views or suggestions of the local bodies assigned a role in planning.

issues.definition: A town development scheme that reconstitutes land is invalid when the formulating authority bypasses the local planning bodies assigned a role in the planning process.

issues.legal_issue: A development plan cannot be revised without considering the district plans that the governing law requires the planning authority to take into account.
material_facts: The planning authority revised the master plan to suit the proposed scheme.
The record did not show that the authority considered a draft five-year plan or annual development plan prepared for the district.
The revised plan was used to support the scheme.
issues.conclusion: The revision was unlawful and required reconsideration under the prescribed legal procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 14 and 17 of the 1973 Act govern preparation of development plans and require consideration of district plans prepared under the Madhya Pradesh Zila Yojana Samiti Adhiniyam, 1995. Article 243ZD provides for district planning. The Court also relied on Chairman, Indore Vikas Pradhikaran v. Pure Industrial Coke & Chemicals Ltd. for the relationship between development plans and master plans.

predicates.development_plan_revision: A planning authority has revised a development plan or master plan.
predicates.required_district_plans_not_considered: The authority did not consider the district plans that the governing law requires it to take into account.

issues.definition: A revision of a development plan is unlawful and requires reconsideration when the authority fails to consider the required district plans.

issues.legal_issue: An official's participation in proposing and approving the same land expansion vitiates the approval when the decision lacks independent and objective consideration.
material_facts: The same official proposed a major expansion of the scheme while serving in the development authority and later approved that proposal while serving in the state government.
The expansion was approved shortly after it was proposed.
The record showed no prior survey or assessment supporting the expansion and no independent application of mind by the approving government.
issues.conclusion: The approval was tainted by bias and non-application of mind and was invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Administrative action must comply with natural justice and be free from bias; a person should not judge their own cause. The Court relied on Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner, A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India, State of Punjab v. Gurdial Singh, and M/s J. Mohapatra & Co. v. State of Orissa. It noted the doctrine of necessity as a limited exception where no other competent decision-maker is available.

predicates.land_development_scheme: A public authority is considering an expansion of a land development scheme.
predicates.same_official_proposed_and_approved_expa: One official participated in proposing the expansion and later participated in approving it in another official capacity.
predicates.no_independent_review: The approving authority did not independently and objectively assess the proposal.

issues.definition: Approval of a land-scheme expansion is vitiated when the same official proposes and approves it without independent review.

issues.legal_issue: The power to declare an intention to prepare a town development scheme is constrained by the scheme's planning purpose and cannot be exercised arbitrarily without a reasoned assessment of need.
material_facts: The scheme's proposed area changed substantially and repeatedly without reasons supported by a survey or assessment of need.
The development authority produced no survey or report substantiating the stated population and land requirement.
The state government approved the expanded proposal without independent objective consideration.
issues.conclusion: The scheme was not prepared in accordance with the statutory procedure and was ultra vires.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 49 and 50 of the 1973 Act govern the purposes and preparation of town development schemes. The phrase permitting action at any time does not confer unfettered discretion; the scheme must implement a development plan and be based on proper planning. The Court relied on Chairman, Indore Vikas Pradhikaran v. Pure Industrial Coke & Chemicals Ltd., Bondu Ramaswamy v. Bangalore Development Authority, and Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation v. Ahmedabad Green Belt Khedut Mandal.

rule.if: town_development_scheme and (no_prior_need_assessment or unexplained_area_changes) and no_independent_state_review

predicates.town_development_scheme: A development authority proposes a town development scheme.
predicates.no_prior_need_assessment: The authority did not conduct a survey or assessment establishing the need and extent of the proposed scheme before proposing it.
predicates.unexplained_area_changes: The proposed scheme area changed substantially without documented reasons supporting those changes.
predicates.no_independent_state_review: The state government approved the proposal without independently and objectively considering its basis.

issues.definition: A town development scheme is ultra vires when it lacks a prior assessment of need or has unexplained changes in scope and receives no independent state review.

issues.legal_issue: A town development scheme cannot be prepared in the absence of the zoning plan that provides detailed land-use particulars.
material_facts: No zoning plan was in place when the scheme was formulated.
The scheme assigned detailed uses to land and sought changes to the master plan to accommodate its proposed development.
The master plan did not specify land use with sufficient detail for the scheme.
issues.conclusion: The scheme could not lawfully be formulated without a zoning plan and was invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 17, 20, 21 and 49 of the 1973 Act establish a hierarchy in which a development plan provides the broader framework, a zoning plan specifies land uses in detail, and a town development scheme implements that planning. The Court relied on Chairman, Indore Vikas Pradhikaran v. Pure Industrial Coke & Chemicals Ltd. and on the statutory purpose of ensuring effective preparation and execution of development and zoning plans.

predicates.town_development_scheme: A development authority proposes a town development scheme.
predicates.zoning_plan_absent: No zoning plan has been prepared for the area covered by the scheme.
predicates.scheme_assigns_detailed_land_uses: The scheme specifies detailed uses for land that are not established by an applicable zoning plan.

issues.definition: A town development scheme that assigns detailed land uses is invalid when no zoning plan exists for the area.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory committee must provide a meaningful hearing and a complete assessment of the matters prescribed for a plot-reconstitution scheme.
material_facts: The committee's report omitted assessments concerning contributions, changes in plot value, and compensation, and treated those matters as inapplicable without valid reasons.
The scheme's layout had been prepared and approved before the committee finished hearing objections.
The objections were rejected without adequate reasons or a genuine opportunity to be heard.
issues.conclusion: The committee process did not comply with mandatory statutory requirements and vitiated the scheme.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 50(5) and 50(6) of the 1973 Act require consideration of objections and suggestions, a hearing for persons who seek one, and a report addressing prescribed matters, including plot values, contributions, and compensation. The Court relied on Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation v. Ahmedabad Green Belt Khedut Mandal, Raghbir Singh Sehrawat v. State of Haryana, and Indore Development Authority v. Madan Lal.

predicates.plot_reconstitution_scheme: A town development scheme involves reconstitution of plots and requires review by a statutory committee.
predicates.committee_report_incomplete: The committee omits prescribed assessments or declares them inapplicable without valid reasons.
predicates.objections_prejudged_or_not_fairly_heard: The objections are decided before the hearing is complete or are rejected without a fair hearing and objective consideration.

issues.definition: A plot-reconstitution scheme is vitiated when the statutory committee omits required assessments or does not fairly hear and consider objections.

issues.legal_issue: Plot reconstitution under the governing law is limited to specified public purposes and does not confer a general power to rearrange private land for a housing scheme.
material_facts: The development authority sought to reconstitute land for a general township and housing scheme.

The governing state statute authorized plot reconstitution for buildings, roads, drains, sewage lines, and similar amenities but did not create an authority to adjust landowners' property rights for a general housing scheme.
The statute contained no procedure empowering an official to transfer or rearrange those property rights for that broader purpose.
issues.conclusion: Plot reconstitution was permissible only for the specified public purposes and could not be undertaken for a different purpose such as a general housing scheme.
issues.legal_principle: Section 49(viii) of the 1973 Act allows provision for reconstitution of plots for buildings, roads, drains, sewage lines, and similar amenities. Unlike the Gujarat and Maharashtra statutes discussed by the Court, the applicable law did not establish an officer empowered to alter property rights through plot reconstitution. The Court relied on Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation v. Ahmedabad Green Belt Khedut Mandal in discussing the distinct statutory procedure for plot reconstitution under another statute.

predicates.plot_reconstitution: A public authority rearranges or reconstitutes privately owned plots.
predicates.purpose_not_specified_public_utility: The reconstitution is for a purpose other than the specified public amenities or similar public utilities.
predicates.no_statutory_power_to_adjust_property_ri: The governing law does not empower an authority to adjust or transfer the landowners' property rights for that purpose.

issues.definition: Plot reconstitution is not authorized when it serves a purpose beyond specified public utilities and the governing law grants no power to alter property rights for that purpose.

issues.legal_issue: Land acquisition cannot be justified by returning an arbitrarily determined minority share of developed land while retaining the rest as a development contribution without lawful assessment and adequate compensation.
material_facts: The authority proposed returning only 35% of the reconstituted plots to landowners and retaining 65% for other purposes.
The returned percentage was not supported by a valid calculation based on land values and locations, and the percentage varied among landowners.
The authority sought to retain land as a development contribution without an assessment of the accrued increase in value.
issues.conclusion: The authority was not justified in returning only 35% of the reconstituted plots and retaining 65%; the arrangement was constitutionally impermissible and inconsistent with the statutory limit on development contributions.
issues.legal_principle: Article 300A protects the right to property. Section 50(6)(vi) of the 1973 Act limits a development contribution to half of the accrued increment in value. The Court relied on Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala concerning compensation and explained that it did not follow the earlier approach in State of Gujarat v. Shantilal Mangaldas; it also applied Section 50(6)(vi).

predicates.compulsory_land_acquisition: The state or a public authority compulsorily takes privately owned land for a development scheme.
predicates.return_share_arbitrary: The authority returns only a portion of developed land without a valid assessment and without a rational basis for the allocation.
predicates.retained_contribution_exceeds_half_of_as: The authority retains a development contribution exceeding half of the properly assessed increase in value.

issues.definition: A compulsory acquisition arrangement is unjustified when the returned share is arbitrary or the retained development contribution exceeds half of the properly assessed increase in value.

issues.legal_issue: A development project requiring environmental clearance cannot proceed on a clearance granted by an incompetent authority or after a material change in scope without the required fresh clearance.
material_facts: The township project fell within a category requiring environmental clearance.
The project was in a severely polluted area for which the applicable procedure required central-level consideration.
The project sought clearance for a larger area than the area ultimately covered by the scheme, and the project scope and land-use arrangements later changed.
No fresh environmental clearance was obtained for the changed project scope.
issues.conclusion: The project failed to obtain the required environmental clearance, which was a mandatory requirement for initiating it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the environmental clearance requirements under the Ministry of Environment and Forests notification of 14 September 2006, the applicable categorization of township and area-development projects, and the memoranda governing clearance in severely or critically polluted areas. It also relied on the clearance condition requiring fresh approval if the project scope changed.

predicates.environmental_clearance_required: The kind of development project requires environmental clearance before it can proceed.
predicates.clearance_granted_by_incompetent_authori: The clearance was granted by an authority that was not competent under the applicable environmental procedure.
predicates.project_scope_changed_without_fresh_clea: The project materially changed after clearance was sought or granted, and no fresh clearance was obtained for the changed scope.

issues.definition: A project lacks valid environmental clearance when clearance was required but was granted by an incompetent authority or the project materially changed without fresh clearance.
